Triggers.value: Visible injuries or wounds on others

Maladaptive Strategies.value: avoid relaxing because it feels dangerous
Any form of physical contact with others

Memory.value: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.
The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to

I am permanently an outsider now
People are not what they seem

issues.explanation: The trigger pattern is only partly coherent with the trauma type and the rest of the profile. Nausea and visible injuries fit partner physical abuse, but darkness is a more context-specific trigger that is not supported by the memory or appraisal items; no item suggests assaults occurring in dark spaces or fear linked to darkness specifically.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Public Transport: Using public transport
issues.explanation: Avoiding public transport is hard to explain from the rest of the profile. None of the trigger, memory, or appraisal items point to buses/trains/crowds/public transit as trauma-linked cues, so this strategy appears to target a symptom context not otherwise represented in the profile.

issues.item: Triggers: Male Presence: Being alone with men
issues.explanation: For trauma type 'physical abuse by romantic partner,' the trigger 'being alone with men' is hard to reconcile unless the abusive partner was male and the fear generalized specifically to men; demographics/trauma description do not support that specificity, so this item is clinically questionable.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Mistrust: People can't be trusted
issues.explanation: The appraisal 'People can't be trusted' is very broad and non-specific, while the trigger pattern is specifically male-coded. That combination is not impossible, but here it weakens coherence because the profile gives no corresponding trauma-linked reason for a male-specific trigger alongside a fully generalized interpersonal belief.

Within the Memory node, 'hard to deliberately recall' and 'memories are very clear and detailed' can coexist in PTSD, but in this profile they are phrased in a way that risks direct contradiction unless the distinction between involuntary vivid intrusions and impaired voluntary recall is explicit. A clinician would likely question whether these two items were selected to describe the same memory pattern without additional clarification.

vignette: Elias Vance had been twenty-four when the living room floor became a landscape of broken glass and bruised knuckles. It began during a dispute over finances, but it was the physicality that remained etched in his days. Now, at twenty-six, the precinct air still carries that same tension. As a detective, Elias spends his days moving through rooms where injuries are routinely examined. When he photographs a victim’s split lip or traces the contusion on a suspect’s forearm, a wave of nausea rises in his throat. It is the specific texture of broken skin under fluorescent lights that catches him. At home, the scent of his wife’s nightly wine seeps through the hallway. The aroma alone tightens his stomach. He keeps his meals light and his windows open during dinner, the smell arriving unbidden, sharp and unmistakable. The memories do not wait for permission to surface. They arrive with startling clarity, fully formed and detailed, as if he were standing in that living room again. He hears the specific crack of the table, the low timbre of his wife’s voice, the heavy sigh that followed the first strike. The sounds press against his temples, uncontrolled, forcing themselves into his thoughts whether he is reviewing case files or standing in the shower. He has come to believe that the event altered the ground beneath his feet. He feels permanently set apart, an outsider watching the world move through a pane of glass. When colleagues offer condolences or share stories of their own families, he listens quietly. He is certain that people are not what they seem. Their smiles are practiced, their assurances provisional. He has lost his faith in the idea that safety is a steady state. This quiet distance has shaped how he moves through his routine. He avoids relaxation; stillness feels dangerously close to being caught off guard. He sits on the edge of chairs, keeps his keys within reach, and never truly unwinds. Physical contact, whether a colleague’s hand on his shoulder or his wife’s arm brushing his during an evening walk, is met with a subtle retreat. He does not pull away sharply. He simply makes room for himself, preserving the space between bodies. His feelings remain present but distant, wrapped in a steady emotional numbness. He functions through his days without being overwhelmed. He reads the precinct case reports with detached precision, noting facts without letting them settle deep. Over the past six months, the accumulation of these habits has reshaped his days. He takes longer routes to the station to avoid crowded corridors where he might encounter someone with a visible scar. He declines casual invitations to pubs, the clink of glasses and the rising volume of conversation mimicking the atmosphere of the night the incident occurred. His marriage endures, but the quiet negotiations of daily life require careful navigation. He sleeps in the guest room two nights a week, finding the distance necessary rather than punitive. Elias sought help when a routine domestic assault call mirrored his own history with startling exactness. Standing in a neighbor’s hallway, watching a man nurse a bleeding knuckle, the nausea returned, the wine scent drifted from a passing passerby, and a voice from the past echoed in his mind. His intake form listed a PCL5 score of 72, a number that reflected the weight he carried daily. He came to the clinic hoping to understand what is happening to his body and his mind, not to erase the past, but to make room for a life that feels entirely his own. He fears that without intervention, the outsider status will harden into permanence, but he trusts that with time, the nausea will settle, the memories will lose their urgency, and the world will once again feel like a place he can touch without flinching.
